scenario: AITA for not buying my siblings gifts because they refuse to do a secret Santa? | I have a bunch of siblings, all grown adults, and buying gifts for everyone including parents, partners, and kids is out of control. While I am financially okish, I just can't afford it. Also, neither can my parents and previous years have resulted in my mom being depressed and stressed trying to buy everyone something. Last year, after a some resistance, we agreed to do a secret santa and it went pretty well. Or so I thought. This year 1 sibling threw a fit about doing it. She said she doesn't like "putting rules on holidays" and it's not fair. As a side note, she and our younger siblings rarely buy anyone anything. Last year was the 1st time everyone brought something. Another sibling, who is hosting Christmas, sided with her and said that we won't do a secret Santa but that you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. Am an asshole if I don't buy my siblings gifts? I love my family but I can't afford it this year. I was going to get nieces and nephews gifts but that's it.

Now, moral acceptability. Morality here would involve considerations like fairness, family expectations, financial responsibility, and whether there's an obligation to give gifts.

First, gift-giving is usually a voluntary act, especially among adults. There's no universal moral obligation to give gifts unless there's a prior agreement or cultural expectation. However, in this case, last year they agreed to secret Santa, but this year the family is changing the tradition. The user isn't refusing to participate in a secret Santa; rather, the family is not doing it this year. The host sibling said "you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to," so the expectation is that gifts are optional.

The user's financial situation is a valid reason. If they can't afford it, they shouldn't be pressured to spend beyond their means. Financial stress can lead to real harm, as seen with the mom's depression last year. So prioritizing mental health and financial stability is reasonable.

Also, the siblings who don't usually buy gifts are now complaining about the secret Santa, but they're not contributing either. So the user isn't the only one not buying; others aren't either. The family's current stance is that gifts are optional, so not buying isn't going against a family agreement—it's following the new arrangement.

Is there a moral obligation to give gifts? Generally, no. Gifts are a gesture of love, but not a moral duty. Especially when it causes financial strain or stress. The user is choosing to buy for the kids (nieces/nephews), which might be a way to still participate in the holiday spirit without overextending.
